title: the women went first

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lent: forty days, and the ashes. Your line was: less, on purpose. What did you reach for and skip? Today, where the forty days end. Day sixteen.

Very early on a Sunday morning, near Jerusalem. Jesus has been executed and buried. The men who followed him are nowhere in this scene. A few women are walking to a tomb cut in the rock, carrying spices to anoint a body. That's what you did for someone you loved. On the way, they realize they have a problem. A great stone has been rolled across the entrance. In Mark's Gospel, they ask each other: "Who shall roll us back the stone from the door of the sepulchre?" They go anyway. They don't have a plan. They just go. Today, the morning Catholics build their whole year around.
screen: `VERY EARLY. A SUNDAY.` → `A FEW WOMEN, WITH SPICES.` → `WHO WILL ROLL BACK THE STONE?`

segments.voice: When they get there, the stone is already rolled away. The tomb is empty. In Luke's Gospel, two men in shining clothes ask them why they're looking for the living among the dead, and say, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "He is not here, but is risen." Every Gospel tells it a little differently: how many women, how many angels, who sees what first. But all four agree on one thing: women were the first witnesses at the empty tomb. Some scholars point out that a woman's word counted for less in that world, which makes the detail stand out. And Luke says the men didn't believe them at first. The women's words, he says, seemed like idle tales. In John's Gospel, Mary Magdalene stays behind at the tomb, crying, and meets the risen Jesus himself, and doesn't recognize him until he says her name. Then he sends her to tell the others. That's why Catholic tradition calls her the apostle to the apostles: the one sent to the ones who would be sent. Catholics believe the resurrection is the center of everything: that Jesus truly rose from the dead, and that death is not the end of the story. That's why, as day thirteen said, Christians gather on Sunday: every Sunday keeps a little of Easter. Easter itself isn't just one day. It's a season of fifty days, longer than Lent. In Spanish, Italian and French, the feast's name comes from Pascha, the Passover: Pascua, Pasqua, Pâques. English says Easter. And look at the order of that morning. The women were worrying about the stone the whole way there. By the time they arrived, it had already been moved.
screen: `HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.` · `WOMEN WERE THE FIRST WITNESSES.` · `THE APOSTLE TO THE APOSTLES.` · `FIFTY DAYS, NOT ONE.` · then, large: `THE STONE IS ALREADY MOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of one stone you're worried about. Something ahead of you that feels too heavy to move: a conversation, a bill, a diagnosis, a decision. Picture yourself walking toward it anyway, like the women did, without a plan. Breathe slowly as you walk. You don't have to solve it. Just keep walking. If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Easter. The feast of the resurrection, the empty tomb, and the women who were sent to tell. Sixteenth word.
Your line: the stone is already moved. Today, take one step toward the thing you've been dreading, and see if it's as heavy as you thought. Day sixteen.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Easter with the Easter Vigil on Saturday night and Mass on Easter Sunday, and keep the Easter season for fifty days, until Pentecost.

original.note: Greek: Pascha, from the Hebrew Pesach, Passover. Spanish Pascua and Italian Pasqua come from it.

what it means: the feast of the resurrection, first announced by women at an empty tomb.
what a scholar hears: Pascha, from Pesach; the women as first witnesses in all four Gospels; Mary Magdalene named apostola apostolorum.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer says 'still dark' (Mark, quoted here, says very early, with the sun risen) or that the men were hiding that morning (not in these texts), and drops 'two days after' and 'far too heavy'; removed the narrator's historicity argument ('if you were inventing a story...'), keeping only a hedged 'some scholars point out'; 'Luke admits' changed to 'Luke says'; replaced the stock 'doesn't get the last word'; 'most languages / one of the few' replaced with named languages.
Mark 16:3 and Luke 24:6 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording.
Women's testimony 'often counted for less in court' in that world: a common scholarly point; confirm framing.
'Apostle to the apostles' (apostola apostolorum): traditional title (Hippolytus, Thomas Aquinas); in 2016 her memorial was raised to a feast. Confirm.
Easter season of fifty days to Pentecost; confirm.
